text: ← Foundations contents THE LEARNING PATH WHAT YOU WILL LEARNCalculate the energy and wavelength of Lyman alpha from hydrogen levels. 01Atoms have discrete energy levels A hydrogen electron cannot have just any bound-state energy. We take the energy-level formula supplied by quantum theory as our starting point. The integer n is 1, 2, 3, …; zero energy corresponds to a separated electron and proton. A level difference becomes photon energyHydrogen emits a 10.2 eV photon when it goes from n = 2 to n = 1. The horizontal lines show state energies, not electron trajectories in space.View larger diagram ↗ En ≈ −13.6 eVn2 A simple hydrogen model, neglecting fine structure and other small corrections. 02What does a 2 → 1 transition emit? Eγ = E2 − E1 = −3.4 − (−13.6) = 10.2 eV λ = hcEγ ≈ 1240 eV·nm10.2 eV ≈ 121.6 nm This is Lyman alpha (Lyα), an ultraviolet line strongly absorbed by Earth’s atmosphere. It is a valuable tracer of cosmic hydrogen. The 2 → 1 transition is not ionization: removing an electron from the ground state requires about 13.6 eV. 03The same idea as the Rydberg formula 1λ = RH(1nlow2 − 1nhigh2) RH ≈ 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹. “High” and “low” label the upper and lower levels. Divide the energy difference by hc to obtain this expression. It is the same energy conservation statement written in terms of wavelength. 04Atomic fingerprints on a continuous spectrum Hot, optically thick matter emits a nearly thermal continuum. Foreground gas can absorb photons at selected transition energies, producing absorption lines. Emission from dilute gas can produce bright lines. Line strength depends on temperature, ionization, and radiation transport as well as abundance. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. What energy is emitted in hydrogen’s n = 3 → 2 transition? Is it ultraviolet? Show the answer and reasoning 13.6 × (1/4 − 1/9) ≈ 1.89 eV. Its wavelength is about 656 nm: the red, visible Hα line.
